Abstract
With the rise of LLMs, GPU acceleration has become essential for both train-
ing and serving AI models. This requires HPC systems to be highly flexible with 
assigning multi-GPU nodes while also maintaining high security standards. Exist-
ing approaches involve utilizing nodes with batch and service schedulers, e.g., 
Slurm and Kubernetes, by dynamically moving nodes between the schedulers either 
through negotiation between the systems or via an external system. However, such a 
multi-use approach also increases the attack surface as more scheduling components 
operate with root permission. Moreover, it becomes increasingly difficult to recover 
from a security incident as attackers might have infected parts of either scheduling 
system. In this work, we present Ephemeral Kubernetes as a way to dynamically 
deploy and remove Kubernetes clusters in Warewulf managed environments such 
that nodes can be booted to be either part of a Slurm or Kubernetes cluster while 
being wiped at shutdown.
Keywords  HPC · Kubernetes · Warewulf · Service · Security · Scheduling
1  Introduction
Modern HPC systems face numerous challenges as workloads require them to be 
evermore flexible [1] while maintaining high security standards [2]. One significant 
trend is the need to support containerization and service workloads [3, 4] without 
losing backwards compatibility for existing workloads or compromising security.
Specifically Slurm [5] and Kubernetes [6] stand out as widespread solutions for 
batch scheduling and container orchestration [7], respectively. Ideally, it would be

In this work, we present Ephemeral Kubernetes as an alternative approach to 
deliver native Kubernetes performance in HPC environments. We utilize Warewulf 
(WW) [15] to boot a set of nodes into either control or worker nodes to form a tem-
porary Kubernetes cluster, which can serve a given workload before rebooting the 
nodes to delete the cluster and return them to their original state.
WW is already a common part of the HPC software stack [16] as it enables 
admins to deliver identical software stacks to a large range of nodes while also 
shipping individual configurations. Our work builds on this to deliver minimal OS 
images, which only ship the software required for the respective workloads, e.g., 
Kubernetes, as described by [3].
There is a high demand for GPU resources in HPC centers as these are required 
for both large language model (LLM) training and inference [17]. Training and infer-
ence necessitate different scheduling approaches, training requires a set of nodes for 
a fixed time block, while an inference service can and needs to adjust the number of 
active instances to match request volumes. With Ephemeral Kubernetes, it is pos-
sible to set up and expand a Kubernetes-based inference cluster next to a regular 
Slurm cluster used for training.
Moreover, we consider this an improvement in terms of security due to the reduc-
tion of attack surface by only including the required software as well as due to the 
built-in cleanup mechanism of completely wiping the nodes during reboot. By reset-
ting the nodes when switching to and from running Kubernetes, a manual cleanup, 
as performed by [4], is avoided. Thus any leftover files or configurations, such as 
IP-tables created by Kubernetes or any other software running on the nodes, are 
removed, eliminating any lingering security risks.
Rebooting nodes into different software stacks significantly improves the security 
as opposed to keeping software stacks and network configurations for training and 
inference or service operation on the same node images. Besides left-over files being 
removed, there is also a more clear distinction of user access patterns. In regular 
HPC environments [16], users have shell access via SSH to a shared set of nodes, 
while users of (inference-) service platforms expect web and API interfaces. These 
two access patterns come with vastly different assumptions about security, i.e., what 
attack surfaces exist and how they can be protected. For example, HPC users with 
shell access might be able to send requests to internal Kubernetes API endpoints, 
which are only secured via firewalls against access attempts from the public internet. 
This can be solved by having a clear separation of software and network configura-
tions via separate node images for training and service.
Ephemeral Kubernetes consists of two WW node images, one for control nodes 
and one for worker nodes as well as a WW system overlay. The overlay includes 
an installer script that deploys and configures Kubernetes on the respective nodes 
as well as a Python script running as a Systemd service, which is deployed on the 
control nodes to setup and update HAProxy [18]. Together with Keepalived [19] this

2  Related work
The need for HPC systems to become more flexible to support a larger range of 
workload types is a common problem [1, 3]. This often breaks down to extending 
an existing HPC batch scheduling system to support container orchestration or to 
extend a cloud container orchestration system to be able to utilize HPC resources 
[8].
While Ephemeral Kubernetes does not provide an integration with Slurm or any 
other batch scheduler in its current form, it depends on WW, a common component 
of HPC infrastructures [16]. Its conceptually similar to [4], i.e., it enables the usage 
of HPC nodes for cloud workloads that require a container orchestrator.

•	 Slurm under Kubernetes: Here the infrastructure is managed by Kubernetes and

•	 Kubernetes under Slurm: In this approach the infrastructure is operated by Slurm

•	 Other approaches: These include works that do not utilize Kubernetes or any

Regarding the subsection names, it should be noted that Slurm is the most common 
batch scheduler for these studies but not everywhere while Kubernetes is almost 
omnipresent with only a few works considering alternatives such as Apache Mesos 
[21].
2.1  Slurm under Kubernetes
In [9] the authors argue for the containerization of HPC schedulers in order to 
improve the elasticity in terms of being able to adapt to the addition or removal of 
compute resources. A similar approach is presented in [11], where the authors show-
cased how to run various batch schedulers on top of Kubernetes including OpenPBS 
[22], OAR [23] and Slurm.
The authors of [24] identified issues with scheduling in Kubernetes related to net-
work performance due to workloads consisting of multiple components that closely 
interact with each other being scheduled across multiple nodes. Via an adjusted 
scheduling strategy based on grouping deployments in the same Kubernetes names-
pace together, the authors showcased improved performance via containerized 
Slurm running on their Kubernetes cluster.
Another approach to improve the resource utilization was presented by the 
authors of [14]. In their case for Slurm running on top of Kubernetes. For this they 
set up a scheduling system that is able to identify gaps besides Slurm workloads and 
inserts Kubernetes workloads into these gaps.
2.2  Kubernetes under Slurm
In [10] and [8] the authors present High-Performance Kubernetes (HPK) [25], 
which enables Kubernetes clusters to submit workloads to Slurm. The submitted 
workloads are then executed via Singularity [26] or Apptainer [27] inside of Slurm 
jobs. However, the workloads running via Slurm cannot provide some network-
ing features such as Kubernetes services as they cannot properly integrate with the

the Kubernetes cluster.
In the approach given in [4], the authors configure HPC nodes as Kubernetes 
workers and join them to an external Kubernetes. The configuration is done via the 
existing HPC scheduler, which sets up the Kubernetes dependencies before joining 
the nodes to the external Kubernetes cluster. After the Kubernetes worker job con-
cludes in the HPC scheduler, the nodes are cleaned up by removing the configura-
tions made by the cluster as well as leftover files.
2.3  Other approaches
In another previous research effort [33], we did not deploy Kubernetes at all but 
instead wrote a service scheduling system on top of Slurm, which enables the 
deployment of constantly running deployments on HPC nodes via Slurm jobs. 
While this approach worked for us to deliver a functional and scalable service, we 
ended up re-implementing many features that were already included in Kubernetes. 
However, as we completely relied on Slurm, this also enabled the HPC hardware to 
be shared between our service platform and regular HPC workloads.
Another approach without Kubernetes is presented in [34] via a co-scheduling 
approach. Here Slurm is used in combination with Apache Mesos where the sched-
uling system is able to identify gaps into which Mesos can schedule workloads.
The Kubernetes scheduler is intended for container orchestration and makes 
assumptions about the workloads it schedules accordingly. For example, when 
two workloads each request four instances to be deployed and the cluster only has 
enough resources for six such instances, the default Kubernetes scheduler will assign 
three instances each. However, as discussed by [7], HPC workloads often require 
gang scheduling, where a certain number of instances belonging to the same work-
load must be deployed before the workload can start operating at all. In the above

2.4  Performance & security
For HPC performance is essential [2]. In order to provide such performance, the 
overhead imposed by any system must be minimal such that as much compute power 
as possible is available to user workloads.
HPC systems are commonly multi-user systems [16] where regular users have 
limited permission to install software and reconfigure nodes. Root access permission 
are reserved for trusted administrators who maintain the system. This security para-
digm is, therefore, dependent on users not being able to install or invoke software, 
which might grant them root permission.
Given these limitations, the need for support for running container virtualization 
in HPC environments [3] have to be balanced against the security concerns [39] that 
installing container runtimes that operate as root bring. Apptainer as shown by [10] 
provides a middle-ground solution with limited features that operates safely without 
root access.
Ephemeral Kubernetes requires a rootful installation similar to [4] and leaves the 
option open to configure access using Kubernetes internal access controls. A user 
with admin access to a Kubernetes cluster can escalate this to root access on any 
node of the cluster, for example, by deploying a privileged container that mounts /
etc/shadow and replaces the root password. The default user permission should 
therefore be carefully set when giving users access to Kubernetes clusters running in 
HPC environments.
For approaches that operate Slurm on top of Kubernetes, a performance overhead 
is incurred, which especially affects workloads that include significant amounts of 
network communication [40] due to the network virtualization applied by Kuber-
netes. For example, MPI workloads are highly affected by this. This overhead adds

3  Ephemeral Kubernetes
Ephemeral Kubernetes consists of
•	 Build scripts for two WW images, one for worker nodes and one for control 
nodes
•	 A Kubernetes installer script included in the WW system overlay
•	 A Systemd service to configure and maintain a HA setup via HAProxy and Kee-
palived, as well as the rejoining of nodes, called Phylactery, which is included in 
the WW system overlay
Via these components, Ephemeral Kubernetes provides a HA Kubernetes deploy-

3.1  Methodology
The design goals for Ephemeral Kubernetes were to create a solution that has the 
following capabilities.
•	 Deploying standalone Kubernetes clusters
•	 Utilizing common HPC infrastructures
•	 Dynamically handling node additions and removals
•	 Supporting production grade features such as HA Kubernetes
•	 Providing strict security guarantees by design
•	 Quick cluster deployments from scratch
•	 Serve as basis for a hybrid training and inference service HPC platform
Compared to many of the existing solutions discussed in 2, our main focus was on 
security and providing standard Kubernetes clusters to minimize the potential for 
compatibility issues when running production workloads. Moreover, we wanted to 
both support short-running on demand Kubernetes clusters that need to return their

clusters that might need to grow and shrink as needed.
Given these desired capabilities and use cases, WW became the basis for Ephem-
eral Kubernetes as it was already present in many HPC environments [16] and capa-
ble of supporting our desired security guarantees. WW itself is capable of stateless 
node provisioning and per-node configuration upon which we expanded by imple-
menting coordination mechanisms. These mechanisms enable the setup and contin-
gency of a Kubernetes cluster even when individual nodes are rebooted.
We considered also developing an integration with a specific scheduling platform 
such as Slurm but instead focused on Ephemeral Kubernetes as a self-contained 
solution that only relies on WW. The development of such integrations or dynamic 
negotiation platforms similar to [37], which could better support the use case of long 
running service clusters next to Slurm clusters, are future research efforts in our 
view.
The Phylactery service was added to solve the problem of setting up and main-
taining a Kubernetes control plane where nodes may be added or rebooted anytime. 
When adding nodes, this involves extending the coverage of the HA setup to the new 
nodes. For rebooted nodes, these nodes need to be de-registered from the cluster 
before they can be added again. This is necessary as Kubernetes and Etcd refuse 
to add nodes that have the same name or IP address as existing members of their 
clusters.
According to the above discussion, for a product to be a valid solution it must be 
able to do the following.
•	 Deploy a vanilla Kubernetes cluster on top of WW
•	 Automatically deploy and maintain a HA Kubernetes control plane
•	 Handle the addition, removal and rebooting of nodes
•	 Quickly deploy across multiple nodes, i.e., avoid unnecessary operations that 
cost significant time
Except for the last point, these can be considered functional requirements that can 
be validated by checking whether the software provides the desired capability. The 
answer to whether a capability is supported is yes or no. Quick deployments can be 
considered a non-functional requirement, which in this case needs to be answered 
by benchmarking the time taken for the deployment stages and estimating whether 
these are acceptable.
3.2  Deployment workflow
As a prerequisite for Ephemeral Kubernetes, Warewulf 4 must be installed (we 
tested version 4.5.8-1 on RockyLinux 9.4) and configured to be able to deploy oper-
ating system images for a number of nodes. The node on which WW is installed 
should be a node reserved for administrators and under sufficient protection as serv-
ing images is a security critical operation.

We assume in the following that all nodes that should deploy Kubernetes con-
trol plane components are named controlN where N is a positive integer, for 
example, control[0-2] would refer to the nodes control0, control1 
and control2. Similar for worker nodes we assume the name workerN. For 
an HA setup there must be at least three control nodes in deployment. In our 
experiment we deployed Kubernetes v1.32.1, which was the most recent version 
as of the time of our experiments.
Furthermore, we configured WW to deploy an NFS share on the nodes, which 
serves to synchronize configurations between the nodes. In our experiment we 
deployed the nodes without internet access and pre-loaded the container images 
onto the NFS such that they could be imported on each node. To avoid repeated 
downloads of the same images, it is beneficial to always pre-load the images 
either onto a shared file storage or registry cache.
In addition to the IPs of the nodes, there is also a virtual IP (VIP) address, 
which is to be used by Keepalived and HAProxy to provide HA access to the 
control plane API. In our setup this IP is set as 10.0.0.99 in Keepalived and 
mapped to vip.kubernetes.local via the hosts setting of each node.
These settings are included into the WW images but could also be loaded 
as part of a system overlay. Moreover, the base image includes Containerd and 
Kubelet along with the CLI tools Kubectl, Helm [41] and Etcdctl [42]. HAProxy 
and Keepalived are only installed into the control images on top of the base 
image, which are to be used for the control plane nodes, while the base image is 
used for the worker nodes.
We use the same system overlay k8s-overlay for all nodes. During the 
setup process, our install script checks the hostname of the node and if the name 
contains ’control’, it will deploy as a control plane node. Alternatively this could 
also be configured via an additional overlay or other node metadata configured 
via WW.
When deploying a Kubernetes cluster, a single control plane node needs to 
initialize the cluster. The initialization involves, among other operations, gener-
ating certificates and tokens, which need to be shared with other control plane 
nodes for them to join the cluster. In the following we refer to the node that per-
forms these operations as Control  (Leader) (as shown in Fig. 1) or short 
leader. Once the initialization has been completed, the leader node operates 
effectively the same as the other control plane nodes that joined the cluster.
Figure  1 shows the major steps of the deployment process as they occur. 
Assuming that all nodes are booting at the same time to form an Ephemeral 
Kubernetes cluster, the respective sequences on all nodes will occur in parallel, 
i.e., Step 1-6 are executed in parallel to Step 7-11 and 12-15 as well as Step 16-18 
and Step 19-20. It is also possible to start a cluster with a single node and to later 
add more nodes as needed.

3, 9, 14 The nodes each execute a oneshot service called k8s-install. This 
service was installed via the system overlay and in turn calls the main installation 
script k8s-install.sh. The install script performs network and kernel con-
figurations required by Kubernetes, which could not be included into the Docker 
build process used by WW as the kernel of the images cannot be changed while 
building with Docker. Alternatively to changing these settings via the install 
script, they could also have been included in the system overlay, for example, via 
a configuration file under /etc/sysctl.d. Finally, the script starts the import 
of container images from the NFS share as shown in 1. This is the last step that is 
identical for all nodes.
4, 10 All control nodes attempt to create the leader file, which is a simple text 
file containing the hostname of the node that created it. Via this race, the node 
that reaches this point first becomes responsible for initializing the Kubernetes 
cluster, while the other nodes have to wait for it to be ready before they can join. 
This step is given in Fig. 1 as "Try to create leader file" where the node that will 
be leader is the one that succeeds. Before this point, any of the control nodes 
could have become leader.
As the leader is decided by multiple nodes attempting to create a file on an 
NFS share, there is the possibility of multiple nodes succeeding before the NFS 
properly synchronizes the file creation even if it runs in sync mode. However, 
during the previous step of the install scripts, the import of the container image 
takes multiple seconds with slight fluctuations due to the parallel network opera-
tions on the NFS. Due to this, the timing is already slightly dispersed such that 
it becomes unlikely that multiple leaders will emerge. In our experiments we 
could not produce this event so we assume that it is rare enough to be ignored.
Nevertheless, in order to ensure that only exactly one leader emerges even for 
high numbers of control nodes, another schema could be implemented. For exam-
ple, all nodes could write their hostname or IP as files into the same folder on 
the NFS share. After a short timeout, which ensures that the NFS had time to 
synchronize the folder between the nodes, for example, 2 s, the leader would 
be chosen based on whatever file has the oldest timestamp. The leader election 
would then be marked as concluded by creating another file such that nodes that 
join later do not need to wait for the timeout but instead can immediately identify 
the leader. With this approach, the initial deployment takes longer equal to the 
timeout chosen. A more sophisticated consensus and leader election algorithm 
such as Raft [43] could be used but is not required to only find an initial leader.
11, 15 All control nodes that are not leader wait for the leader node to cre-
ate a file called leader_ready to signal that the cluster is up. Worker nodes 
do not attempt to create the leader file and also wait for the leader_ready 
file to appear. This effectively serves as a synchronization barrier in the parallel 
deployment process.

waits for the Phylactery service to be ready before running kubeadm init to 
deploy Kubernetes. Waiting for the Phylactery service ensures that the VIP for 
the control plane endpoint is reachable, which is required for the Kubernetes con-
trol plane deployment to complete.
The Phylactery service is a Python program, phylactery.py that is shipped with 
the system overlay and deployed as a Systemd service. When it is started, it cre-
ates a file with the hostname and IP address of the current node on the NFS share 
and then checks that folder for any such records from the other nodes. It then con-
structs the new HAProxy configuration, as it requires a list of all nodes to include 
for the HA setup, and installs the configuration and restarts HAProxy.
As more control nodes join, the HAProxy configuration has to be updated on 
every control node to ensure that the HA setup and fail-over properly work. For 
this purpose, the Phylactery service sets up a simple HTTP server, which on 
receiving a GET request will check for new files with hostnames and IPs on the 
NFS share and rebuild the HAProxy configuration. The HTTP server is set up as 
the final step of the service, as the penultimate step, the service sends out requests 
to the HTTP servers of all other Phylactery services in the cluster. This leads to 
all nodes refreshing their HAProxy configuration whenever a new node joins the 
control plane.
Another task handled by the Phylactery service is the proper rejoining of con-
trol nodes. When a node is restarted, no settings are preserved, so the node will 
execute the install script from the beginning. However, if the node was part of 
the cluster before, the cluster will refuse the restarted node to rejoin because the 
cluster already has a member with the same hostname and IP address. Before the 
node can rejoin, the old membership has to be removed both via kubectl for the 
Kubernetes cluster as well as via etcdctl for the Etcd cluster. These steps are per-
formed by the Phylactery service before it marks the node as ready such that the 
installation script waits before attempting to rejoin the node to the cluster.
Worker nodes do not deploy the Phylactery service. In their case, the removal of 
the Kubernetes cluster membership is performed as part of the main install script. 
While we implemented these cleanup steps for the control nodes in the Phylac-
tery service, they could have also been implemented in the main install script to 
the same effect.
The next step for the control leader after running the Phylactery service is to 
deploy Kubernetes via kubeadm. As part of this the control plane components are 
deployed, cluster certificates are generated and the cluster admin configuration is 
created.

In our prototype we used the admin conf file to join other control plane and 
worker nodes to the cluster. With access to this file, kubectl commands can 
be run on the cluster with administrator permission, which can be escalated 
to root permission on the individual nodes. This bears a significant risk, if the 
NFS share is also used by other nodes or if users should only be granted lim-
ited access to the cluster. To mitigate this risk, a token could be used instead 
for joining the nodes. However, the Phylactery service and the main install 
script both use kubectl to handle rejoining, i.e., removing the previous mem-
bership of the same node. Either a configuration with limited access to only 
perform these activities needs to be generated or the WW host needs to receive 
the admin conf from the control leader and expose an endpoint that allows for 
requesting cleanup operations.
For the other control nodes to join the control plane, they require the Kubernetes 
cluster certificates. We let the install script place the certificates on the NFS share 
such that the other nodes can copy them from there. However, while the certifi-
cates do not directly provide admin access to the cluster, they allow a potentially 
malicious node to pose as a member of the control plane and receive and manipu-
late cluster control commands.
Another solution is to let kubeadm upload the certificates into the cluster dur-
ing initialization and to encrypt them using a specified key [45]. By default, the 
certificates expire after 2 h such that control nodes can join during that time and 
download and decrypt the certificates when given the specified key. Should a 
control node join later, it would need to request the certificates to be uploaded 
again, for example, via a new endpoint of the Phylactery service. If all control 
plane nodes that will ever join a given cluster, join in the first two hours of its 
existence, a re-upload of the certificates is not necessary. However, due to the 
nature of Ephemeral Kubernetes nodes, a control plane node that is rebooted also 
needs to retrieve the certificates again. This reduces the security of this approach, 
as each joining control plane node needs to be able to request a re-upload of the 
certificates as well as access to the key for retrieving them. We discuss further 
approaches to secure the access to the admin conf file and the certificates in Sub-
sect. 3.9.
Finally, the control leader node creates the leader_ready file that the other 
nodes have been waiting for and its install script exits.

3.4  Recovery
Nodes deployed via WW do not retain their system state across reboots. Still, 
reboots may be necessary for maintenance or when troubleshooting hardware issues, 
resulting in a node having to rerun the installation script and rejoin the cluster.
Ensuring that control nodes continue to provide an HA control plane is handled 
by the Phylactery service as it removes residual memberships for the Kubernetes 
cluster itself and for the Etcd cluster. Worker nodes only need to remove their previ-
ous membership for the Kubernetes cluster before rejoining, which is handled by the 
install script as the worker nodes do not deploy the Phylactery service.
Kubernetes by default utilizes Etcd as its key-value store, which is able to 
recover from up to (N-1)/2 permanent node failures [46]. When using an HA 
setup with three nodes in a stacked configuration, i.e., Kubernetes control plane 
and Etcd run on the same nodes, one node may fail or be rebooted without caus-
ing any significant interruptions to the control plane functionality. After reboot-
ing, the rejoining control node has to spend time to synchronize data from the 
other nodes before the cluster is able to sustain another node dropping out.
Worker nodes do not deploy any critical cluster components and any failures 
do not affect the overall ability of the cluster to recover. Due to this worker nodes 
can be added or removed as needed. When permanently removing a worker node, 
its membership should also be removed from the Kubernetes cluster.
Given these capabilities, a cluster can be in one of three states.
•	 Stable, all control nodes are active.
•	 Recoverable, up to (N-1)/2 control nodes have failed.
•	 Irrecoverable, more than (N-1)/2 have failed.
In the last case, Etcd data may be incomplete and the quickest way to restore the 
cluster is to clean up the NFS share and to reboot all nodes to recreate the cluster. 
For the cluster to be able to reach the same operation state as before, all relevant 
configurations that were applied should be saved and replayed.

3.5  Evaluation
We verified the functionality of our implementation of Ephemeral Kubernetes 
by deploying a five node Kubernetes cluster in an OpenStack environment. By 
manually restarting control plane and worker nodes, we confirmed that the HA 
setup worked and that nodes were able to rejoin the cluster. With this, we have 
completed the functional requirements described in Subsect. 3.1.
For the non-functional requirement of deployments being reasonably quick, we 
evaluated Ephemeral Kubernetes by measuring the time it takes for significant 
stages of the deployment to complete, which we define as: 
1.	 First control node booted: Any of the control nodes respond on port 22 to an 
attempt to establish a TCP connection. This was measured by using netcat from 
the WW host to test when any of the control nodes would be able to receive a 
TCP handshake on port 22. The connection test should not pose any significant 
overhead as requests are only sent until the first response is received and no actual 
connection is established.
2.	 Leader file created: Any of the control nodes has created the leader file on the 
NFS share. This was measured by checking the file system of the WW host to 
see if the leader file had been created on the NFS share. During these checks, 
the nodes are loading the container images from the NFS share, however, as the 
checks are done locally on the WW host, their impact should be negligible.
3.	 Kubernetes endpoint responsive: The leader node has started the Kubernetes 
API such that it is able to respond to a health check request. This was measured 
by sending GET requests via curl to the health check endpoint of the control plane 
(https://​vip.​kuber​netes.​local:​6443/​healt​hz), which is expected to respond with 
status code 200 once the cluster is up. Until Keepalived and HAProxy have been 
started, these requests will be undeliverable. After that, HAProxy will attempt 
to deliver the requests and fail until the KubeAPI component of the cluster has 
started. As these requests can be quickly rejected, we consider the impact on the 
deployment time to be negligible.
4.	 Leader ready file created: The leader node has created the leader_ready 
file on the NFS share. Similar to the leader file creation check, this also checks 
the file system of the WW host until the file has been created on the NFS share. 
During these checks, the control leader has to upload the Kubernetes certifi-
cates to the NFS share, which are about 50 KB in size. As the checks are done 
locally on the WW host, their impact should be negligible.
5.	 Cluster ready: All nodes in the deployment have joined the cluster and report 
ready status in Kubernetes. This is measured by running kubectl get nodes 
and parsing the output to check if the cluster has all members and all of them 
report ready status. The kubectl commands are processed by the KubeAPI of the 
control nodes that already joined the cluster such that the impact on the nodes 
still joining the cluster should be negligible.

3.6  Applications
With Ephemeral Kubernetes it is possible to quickly deploy Kubernetes clusters 
on demand on WW-managed infrastructure such as many HPC environments. It 
can also be used when experimenting with Kubernetes configurations that poten-
tially break the cluster as by rebooting all nodes, the cluster can be restored. 
To completely reproduce the original cluster, the  applied modifications have 
to be reproducible. This mechanism can also be used to recover from security 
breaches as recreating the cluster ensures that any potential backdoors installed 
by the attackers are removed as long as the WW host remains save.
Ephemeral Kubernetes could also be used as part of a dynamic negotiation 
system as described by [37]. Depending on demand, as observed by an external 
system, nodes would either be added to a Kubernetes or Slurm cluster based on 
the WW image into which they are booted. This also ensures that no traces are 
left on the nodes from the previous assignment. As demand shifts over time, 
nodes could be pulled from either cluster and rebooted to join the other.
Another potential application is for running SecureHPC workloads as defined 
in [48] where the data being processed is highly sensitive and no one, not even 
administrators, are allowed to have access to it. Should the workload require 
Kubernetes for it to be processed, Ephemeral Kubernetes could be used within 
the secure environment created by SecureHPC.
The idea of creating trusted and secure environments can be further extended 
to the inclusion of Trusted Execution Environments (TEE) via Trusted Platform 
Modules (TPM) as discussed in [49]. As Ephemeral Kubernetes node images 
are all shipped from the same WW host, this can be used as the basis for estab-
lishing a chain of trust on the individual nodes. This would enable applications 
involving highly confidential data that can only be accessed by applications 
attested through a chain of trust.

3.7  Phylactery service
The Phylactery service provides capabilities for setting up and maintaining a HA 
Kubernetes cluster by configuring HAProxy on the control plane nodes. To com-
plete the HA setup, Keepalived must also be installed on each control plane node. 
While it in its current form, it relies on the main installation script, the Phylactery 
service and the idea behind it can also be considered as a standalone solution with-
out Ephemeral Kubernetes.
In HAProxy-based HA Kubernetes, requests going to the Kubernetes control 
plane API get load balanced by HAProxy across all control plane nodes. For this to 
properly work, every instance of HAProxy needs to be aware of all control nodes via 
its configuration. When adding control plane nodes, this configuration needs to be 
updated on all nodes and HAProxy needs to be restarted to reload the configuration, 
which can be handled by the Phylactery service or a similar solution.
The Phylactery service works by first discovering the existing configuration on 
the NFS, adding itself to the list of HAProxy servers and then updating its own 
HAProxy configuration. Afterward, it sends a request to the other nodes found in the 
configuration file to inform them that an updated configuration is available. Finally, 
it starts a simple HTTP server on port 9999 that can trigger it to import the configu-
ration from the NFS again upon receiving a HTTP request.
In order to operate, the Phylactery service requires a shared file system to dis-
cover the current configuration as well as the option to host a simple HTTP server, 
which is reachable from the other control plane nodes. The shared file system is 
used to share the current HAProxy configuration, which includes a list of all other 
node IPs on the control plane. If no shared file system is available, this could also be 
solved by extending the Phylactery service to host a copy of the current configura-
tion via a file server on the virtual IP address hosted by Keepalived.
In the current implementation, the simple HTTP server is only used to alert a 
given Phylactery instance that an updated configuration is available on the shared 
file system. If no shared file system is available, the update could be distributed 
by sending it to the HTTP servers instead of an empty HTTP request. However, 
this would enable anyone who can send requests to the server, to be able to sub-
mit a potentially malicious HAProxy configuration without the additional check of 
access permission on the shared file system. When using the Phylactery service this 
way, WW overlays should be used to establish a shared secret between the control 
plane nodes that can be used to validate incoming requests to update the HAProxy 
configuration.
3.8  Limitations
Employing Ephemeral Kubernetes may result in more frequent rebooting of 
nodes, which can cause hidden costs as the power usage of nodes spikes during 
boot [50], which is especially costly for GPU nodes. Moreover, constant reboots 
can also be harmful to hardware components such as HDDs [51]. However,

When only using SSD nodes, which are common in certain HPC configurations

Nevertheless, it should be noted that the cluster creation time of 90 s dem-

consume roughly twice as much power as during idle state. These values are

not available as part of a scientific study, they still serve to give an idea on what 
a deployment of Ephemeral Kubernetes on bare metal HPC nodes would look 
like. Overall, we estimate that the total time to deploy a Kubernetes cluster on 
bare metal HPC nodes using Ephemeral Kubernetes will take the regular startup 
time of the slowest node in the cluster plus one minute for initializing Kuber-
netes and joining all nodes.
It should also be noted that we consider the implementation of Ephemeral 
Kubernetes presented in this work a prototype that serves to showcase the 
concept. Further development and use case specific adjustments are required 
before it is usable out of the box. These considerations are further discussed in 
Subsect. 3.9.
Another limitation is that in the current implementation, when rebooting all 
nodes, the share folder also has to be cleaned up for the new deployment to work 
properly. However, for the install script to perform a cleanup before deploying 
a new cluster it has to detect if the leader file was created by another node 
of the current cluster or if it is from a previous cluster that was wiped. If the 
hostname noted in the leader file is the same as of one of the control nodes 
that node can deduce that it was either rebooted and should rejoin the cluster or 
that it should perform a cleanup and then initialize the cluster. To determine if it 
should rejoin, it can probe for an active cluster by sending requests to the control 
plane endpoint. The other control nodes have to perform a similar check as a 
leader_ready file could be present without a cluster being initialized.
If the leader of the previous cluster is not among the new set of control 
nodes, all control nodes would be stuck waiting for the previous leader node 
to initialize the cluster again. In this case, the control nodes would need to dis-
cover that there is no active cluster despite a leader_ready file existing and 
then identify a leader. One approach would be that the node that first discov-
ers that there is no active cluster, also checks if the node named in the leader 
file exists. If there is no active cluster and the leader is missing, the node 
should perform a cleanup and then fall back to trying to create the leader file 
first along the other nodes. However, there is also the risk that when a control 
node is rebooted while the cluster is an error state such that the KubeAPI is 
unresponsive, the new node may attempt to initialize a new cluster while the old 
cluster is still active and trying to recover.

3.9  Future work
To further advance Ephemeral Kubernetes we consider three areas of improve-
ment: (1) Cleanup, (2) security and (3) configurability.
As discussed in the previous subsection, when rebooting all nodes, it is dif-
ficult to determine what the current state of the cluster is when the nodes find left 
over files from a previous initialization. In the current implementation, a cleanup 
script is required, which needs to be run manually before deploying a new clus-
ter. In a future version of Ephemeral Kubernetes, this cleanup script should be 
integrated with the main installation script along with a probing mechanism that 
is triggered when a leader_ready file is found to check if there is actually an 
active cluster.
The next area of improvement is security as in the current iteration, Ephem-
eral Kubernetes heavily relies on the NFS to distribute sensitive files such as the 
certificates and the admin conf file. A potential approach is to let the leader 
upload these files to a file server on the WW host and to secure the access via a 
cryptographic key pair. The Kubernetes nodes would receive their key via a WW 
overlay, which the install script would then use to authenticate with the file server 
on the WW host.
This could be further secured by only handing out temporary tokens to reboot-
ing nodes such that a node has only a few minutes of time to read the files before 
their token expires. Access to the NFS share, or the file server on the WW host for 
that matter, is only required for a short time when the nodes are being initialized 
until they are able to join the cluster. After that point, they might require access 
to the container images, which only need write-protection but are otherwise not 
sensitive. The install script could even notify the WW host to expire their token 
early once it has joined the cluster or if the deployment crashed.
By implementing this security model, clusters created via Ephemeral Kuber-
netes do not expose any additional details compared to regular Kubernetes clus-
ters once the temporary token for a given node has been expired. For the Phy-
lactery service, the reliance on the shared file system can also be removed as 
described in Subsect. 3.7 such that the shared file system would not be required 
anymore.
Finally, configurability of Ephemeral Kubernetes should be improved. The 
current prototype implementation has many settings that users might want to 
change as hard coded values in its scripts and code. Instead, another script or CLI 
tool could be created that reads from a configuration file provided by the user and 
adjusts the Ephemeral Kubernetes files in the respective WW overlays.
In addition to these internal improvements, integrations with other scheduling 
systems such as Slurm or the creation of resource negotiation system should be 
considered. Slurm, for example, could be expanded to support a special type of 
job that results in the creation of an Ephemeral Kubernetes cluster. Via a resource 
negotiation system, similar to [37], compute nodes could be dynamically moved 
between a Kubernetes service cluster and a Slurm batch cluster by adjusting the 
respective WW configuration.

4  Conclusion
In order to provide higher flexibility for HPC environments that typically only 
provide batch scheduling systems, we have developed Ephemeral Kubernetes. 
We discussed how Ephemeral Kubernetes deploys Kubernetes on WW-managed 
infrastructure, is able to recover from node failures and how it rejoins nodes to 
the cluster. Moreover, we presented the complete workflow of Ephemeral Kuber-
netes deployments, its applications, limitations and potential improvements.
We benchmarked the deployment of a five node Kubernetes cluster and showed 
that the deployment takes on average less than 90 s with about a third of the time 
spent in boot, Kubernetes bootstrap and nodes joining, respectively. The major-
ity of the variance in deployment times comes from the last of these thirds as it 
depends on the last node becoming ready, which in turn depends on the refresh 
timing of the status in Kubernetes.
While Ephemeral Kubernetes could be useful on its own, we consider it as 
a building block for further developments. Any hybrid scheduling approach that 
seeks to dynamically switch nodes between a batch scheduler and Kubernetes 
could employ Ephemeral Kubernetes to quickly setup Kubernetes control plane 
or worker nodes as required.
We plan to further extend Ephemeral Kubernetes to enable proper cleanup on 
node exit as well as improving the security and overall configurability of the sys-
tem. Furthermore, we plan to investigate scheduling systems that can utilize WW 
to boot into specific images based on resource negotiation between service and

Abstract: With the rise of LLMs, GPU acceleration has become essential for both train- ing and serving AI models. This requires HPC systems to be highly flexible with assigning multi-GPU nodes while also maintaining high security standards. Exist- ing approaches involve utilizing nodes with batch and service schedulers, e.g., Slurm and Kubernetes, by dynamically moving nodes between the schedulers either through negotiation between the systems or via an external system. However, such a multi-use approach also increases the attack surface as more scheduling components operate with root permission. Moreover, it becomes increasingly difficult to recover from a security incident as attackers might have infected parts of either scheduling system. In this work, we present Ephemeral Kubernetes as a way to dynamically deploy and remove Kubernetes clusters in Warewulf managed environments such that nodes can be booted to be either part of a Slurm or Kubernetes cluster while being wiped at shutdown.
